Once the compiler picks which overload a call runs, ranked from an exact match down to one that compiles only through a template, that function's exception guarantee is its promise about the program's state if it throws instead of returning. The
promises nothing leaks and every object stays valid, without saying what value it holds. The
promises the state is exactly what it was before the call, as if the call had never run.
on a function is a stronger promise still: that no exception leaves it.

The problem a guarantee solves is the caller who can't tell what a failed call left behind. A route that refuses a blank waypoint partway through a batch may still hold the waypoints added before the failure, a valid route, but not the one the caller asked for, and the caller can't even tell how much of the batch went in. Knowing which guarantee a function gives is as much a part of calling it correctly as knowing its parameters, because the guarantee decides what the caller must check afterwards.

The mechanism behind the strong guarantee is doing the risky work before touching anything: build the replacement in full, where the only step that can throw runs on data nobody else can see yet, then commit it with operations that cannot fail.

You meet these guarantees on every container and route operation the robot performs on a full queue or a bad reading, and the interview question is naming them, saying which one

alone. Which one a function gives is part of its contract, as much as its parameters are, and the caller can't write correct error handling without knowing it. After this
fails, the caller has to decide whether a half-appended route is acceptable, and it can't even tell how much was appended.
Below the basic guarantee is no guarantee at all: after an exception, an invariant may be broken or a resource leaked, and the object can't safely be used again. Above the strong guarantee is the
: the function can't fail. Destructors, deallocation and
must never fail, and neither may copying or moving an exception object (
). The other two guarantees are built from these operations. Klaus Iglberger's
Back to Basics talk on exceptions

(CppCon 2020) sets the default: every function gives at least the basic guarantee, the strong guarantee where that is possible and reasonable, and the nothrow guarantee only where you can keep that promise through every future change.

RAII gives the basic guarantee almost for free. When every resource has an owner, unwinding releases it, as the RAII topic showed, so the only work left is keeping invariants: never leave an object between two related updates when something that can throw runs.

The strong guarantee needs a recipe, and it has one. Do all the work that can throw on the side, on a copy or on new objects the caller can't see yet, and then commit with operations that can't throw. If anything throws before the commit, the side copies are destroyed during unwinding and the original is untouched. The commit is usually a
when they use the default allocator (

move assignment. The rule of five topic used this recipe for copy assignment, as copy-and-swap. The same recipe works for any function that changes state, and the worked example applies it to two containers that must agree.

It has a price. The copy costs time and memory in proportion to the whole object, on every call, even though most calls succeed. For a route of ten waypoints that is nothing; for a map of a million cells updated at 100 Hz it is a design decision. The cheaper alternative is to validate everything first and change the object only once nothing can fail except allocation. That gives the strong guarantee against bad input, the failure you expect, and the basic guarantee against running out of memory.
becomes strong against blank names by checking them all before appending any.
